newsitem.title: CHINA: China says to be short of grain for decades.
newsitem.headline: China says to be short of grain for decades.

text.p: A top Chinese research body on Wednesday warned that China would face shortages of grain for a long time but said the world's most populous nation could feed itself by the middle of the next century.

A shortage of water and arable land was restraining growth in grain yields while China's labour-intensive farm methods limited competitiveness, the research group under the Beijing think tank, the Chinese Academy of Sciences, said in a report.

"Agriculture will be a crucial and weak link that restricts the growth of China's national economy for a fairly long time to come," the Xinhua news agency quoted the National Conditions Analysis and Research Group as saying.
"China will have to deal with shortages of grain," the report said.
China imported 12 million tonnes of grain in 1996, down 42 percent from the year before, official figures show.

Record harvests over the last two years were mainly a result of increases in the state's purchasing price for grain and Beijing could not expect to be competitive on the international grain market, it said.
"China has no advantages over other competitors in grain and oil crops," it said.
Beijing should provide its army of farmers with more small loans and should help train them in the latest technology at vocational schools or through special courses, it said.
China's countryside is carved up into millions of tiny and inefficient family-run plots that rarely use mechanisation.
Technological improvements would help ensure China could feed its huge population -- now at 1.2 billion -- by the middle of the 21st century, the research group said.
"China will be fully capable of providing food for its countrymen by the middle of the next century and become one of the biggest exporters of agricultural products in the world," it said.
Yields could be further boosted by biological engineering and creating hardier and more productive strains of grain, it said.

China earlier this month revised its figure for 1996 grain output to a record 490 million tonnes from 480 million tonnes, saying it had overestimated the impact on the harvest from floods and other natural disasters last year.
Output was about 465 million tonnes in 1995.
Officials have said the record grain output of the last two years was mainly a result of favourable weather and increases in acreage used to grow grain.
